AiSettingsUpdateRequest.description:
Partial. A message cap of zero is meaningful — "no AI for me" — so it is not unset.

**A cost cap must be more than zero** (Batch X7, AI45-05): zero used to mean "no cost
ceiling", and a cleared box saved zero, so clearing it quietly lifted the money ceiling.
Both caps are bounded at four times their defaults (`caps.MAX_MESSAGE_CAP`,
`caps.MAX_COST_CAP_USD`); they were $1,000 and 10,000 a day.
AiSettingsUpdateRequest.title: AiSettingsUpdateRequest

AiStatusResponse.description:
Whether the assistant can work in **this** deployment.

`configured` is false when Railway holds no `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. That is the TMDB
shape — a feature absent from the deployment with the front end unable to say so —
and this is what lets the UI say it plainly instead of failing at the first question.
AiStatusResponse.title: AiStatusResponse

AskResponse.description:
The answer, and what producing it cost — §9.1's "tokens logged".

The token counts are on the wire, not only in the log, because the person paying for
them is the person reading the answer. `costUsd` is a string: it is a decimal, and a
float would round a fraction-of-a-penny call to something that is not what was billed.
AskResponse.title: AskResponse

AuditEntryResponse.description:
One audit row.

``actorName`` is resolved at read time from the joined profile and is ``None`` when
the profile is gone — the row itself outlives it (`DECISIONS.md` #5), so the log
still shows what happened even when it can no longer show who.
AuditEntryResponse.title: AuditEntryResponse

BarcodeCandidateResponse.description:
One possible film for a scanned code.

**A candidate is never an answer.** §3.4 requires a confirmation step, and the risk
note for this batch is explicit that wrong-edition matches are expected — so
`confidence` exists to order this list and for no other purpose.
BarcodeCandidateResponse.title: BarcodeCandidateResponse

BarcodeConfirmRequest.description: What the person decided this barcode is.
BarcodeConfirmRequest.title: BarcodeConfirmRequest

BarcodeCopyResponse.description:
The owned copy a barcode is already on — Batch X10 (CT46-04, #280).

On 10 Oct two copies of *12 Angry Men* were added under one barcode, a 4K and a Blu-ray,
each through the prompt as "another copy", where #101 makes a box holding both one copy.
BarcodeCopyResponse.title: BarcodeCopyResponse

BestReviewedFilmResponse.description: An owned film by its Blu-ray.com review's Overall score, on a format on the shelf (V9).
BestReviewedFilmResponse.title: BestReviewedFilmResponse

BeyondResultResponse.description: A film the search found on TMDB that is not on the shelf — Batch T2.
BeyondResultResponse.title: BeyondResultResponse

BidTrialReport.description: The whole report, written after every film so a stopped trial keeps what it found.
BidTrialReport.title: BidTrialReport

BidTrialResponse.description: The latest trial: its run, and its report so far.
BidTrialResponse.title: BidTrialResponse

BidTrialStartResponse.description: What pressing "Try bid prices" did. Only ``started`` spends anything.
BidTrialStartResponse.title: BidTrialStartResponse

BoxSetCreateRequest.description:
Optionally seeds the set with items, so "create with 4 items" is one call.

§11.3's acceptance is *"Admin creates 'Columbia Noir Vol 4' with 4 items"*. Two calls
would leave a half-built set behind whenever the second failed; one transaction
cannot.
BoxSetCreateRequest.title: BoxSetCreateRequest

BoxSetMemberResponse.description: One disc in the box, with enough of its film to render a row.
BoxSetMemberResponse.title: BoxSetMemberResponse

CalendarMonthResponse.description:
One month's entries, grouped by day — §7.4's "monthly calendar view".

Grouped server-side so the grid does not have to bucket dates in the browser, and so
a month with nothing in it is an explicit empty list rather than a gap the client
infers.
CalendarMonthResponse.title: CalendarMonthResponse

CalendarSubscriptionResponse.description:
The feed path, returned **once**.

The token is hashed at rest and never retrievable again — so this response is the only
time it exists in plaintext, and asking again rotates it. That is what makes an
accidentally-pasted link recoverable.

**A path, not an absolute URL.** The API does not know its own public origin: deriving
it from the request's ``Host`` header would reflect an attacker-controlled value into a
link, and configuring it would mean a new Railway variable — a hosting change this
project keeps explicit. The web app already holds the origin in ``VITE_API_URL`` and
composes the URL there, which is the one place it is known for certain.
CalendarSubscriptionResponse.title: CalendarSubscriptionResponse

ChallengeResponse.description: eBay's expected challenge reply. camelCase written directly — `DECISIONS.md` #6.
ChallengeResponse.title: ChallengeResponse

ChatMessageResponse.description: One rendered turn. `tool_result` rows never reach here — see the router.
ChatMessageResponse.title: ChatMessageResponse

CollectionItemCreateRequest.description:
Add one disc.

Exactly one of ``movieId`` and ``tmdbId`` identifies the film: ``movieId`` when it
is already in the catalogue, ``tmdbId`` when the add form found it on TMDB and the
row has to be created. Two fields rather than one polymorphic id because the two
cases do genuinely different work and a caller always knows which it has.
CollectionItemCreateRequest.title: CollectionItemCreateRequest

CollectionItemResponse.description:
One disc, as the write endpoints return it.

Carries ``movieId`` — which ``CollectionCopyResponse`` does not, because there the
film is already the thing being looked at — so a client that just created an item
knows which film's caches to refresh.
CollectionItemResponse.title: CollectionItemResponse

CollectionItemUpdateRequest.description:
Replace the editable fields of one disc.

A full replacement of a bounded field set rather than a patch: the edit form holds
every one of these, so "absent" unambiguously means "the user cleared it" instead of
being indistinguishable from "the client is an older build that never knew about it".
CollectionItemUpdateRequest.title: CollectionItemUpdateRequest

CollectionMoveEntry.description:
One disc and where it goes — Batch Y2 (`DECISIONS.md` #265).

**Each entry carries its own place**, not one target for the whole request. A move
sends the same place on every entry; "Move them back" sends each disc's own previous
place, through the same endpoint, so the undo is not a second write path. The three
place fields mean what they mean on the copy form, resolved by the same function.
CollectionMoveEntry.title: CollectionMoveEntry

CollectionMoveResponse.description: Batch Y2's partial-success shape, as #6 allows a batch endpoint.
CollectionMoveResponse.title: CollectionMoveResponse

CollectionMoveResult.description: What happened to one disc. A stale or missing disc does not stop the others.
CollectionMoveResult.title: CollectionMoveResult

CollectionValueResponse.description: What the owned discs add up to as used copies, at current eBay asking prices.
CollectionValueResponse.title: CollectionValueResponse

CompletionFilmResponse.description:
One film in a set, owned or not.

``movieId`` is ``None`` for a film that is missing — it has no row in this database,
which is precisely what "missing" means. The title, year and poster therefore come
from the set's cached metadata rather than from ``movies``.
CompletionFilmResponse.title: CompletionFilmResponse

CopyValuationResponse.description: A disc's stored value as a used copy: its film on the format it is valued as.
CopyValuationResponse.title: CopyValuationResponse

CountSlice.description: One wedge, bar or column. ``key`` is the machine value, ``label`` the display one.
CountSlice.title: CountSlice

DailyRunResponse.description: The nightly pass: what it scraped, what it alerted on, what it rolled up.
DailyRunResponse.title: DailyRunResponse

DealResponse.description:
One discounted disc.

**`discountPercent` is arithmetic on the two prices, never a number read off the
page.** The batch's risk note is that a layout change stores a plausible wrong
discount; a figure derived from two prices that each passed a shape check cannot be a
"save 70%" banner that happened to match a selector.
DealResponse.title: DealResponse

DealSourceResponse.description: Batch X2: where deals come from, and when it last answered (UX48-02).
DealSourceResponse.title: DealSourceResponse

DealsRunResponse.description: §5.9's acceptance, as numbers somebody can check against the criterion.
DealsRunResponse.title: DealsRunResponse

DuplicateCheckResponse.description:
Whether this film is already on a shelf, and what the prompt should offer.

``isUpgrade`` is what makes §3.5's acceptance criterion — "adding a 4K when Blu-ray
exists triggers the **upgrade** prompt" — answerable without the web app
re-implementing the format ranking that the database already enforces.
DuplicateCheckResponse.title: DuplicateCheckResponse

EbayAccountResponse.description: Whether connecting is set up, whether this person is connected, and as whom.
EbayAccountResponse.title: EbayAccountResponse

EbayConnectFinishRequest.description: What eBay put on the address it sent the person back to.
EbayConnectFinishRequest.title: EbayConnectFinishRequest

EbayConnectStartResponse.description: Where to send the person to sign in to eBay and agree.
EbayConnectStartResponse.title: EbayConnectStartResponse

EbaySellingResponse.description: The person's listings for sale and what sold in the last 60 days.
EbaySellingResponse.title: EbaySellingResponse

EbayWatchRunResponse.description: The latest scheduled pass, so the page can say when targets were last checked.
EbayWatchRunResponse.title: EbayWatchRunResponse

EbayWatchingResponse.description: The person's watch list and saved searches, as eBay holds them now.
EbayWatchingResponse.title: EbayWatchingResponse

ExistingCopyResponse.description:
One copy already owned, as the duplicate prompt shows it.

§3.5 asks for "existing formats and locations" — exactly these two fields plus
enough to tell two copies of the same film apart.
ExistingCopyResponse.title: ExistingCopyResponse

ExternalFilmResponse.description: The film card for something the collection does not hold — Batch T2.
ExternalFilmResponse.title: ExternalFilmResponse

FilmInCollectionResponse.description: The film a choice would merge into, shown beside the one waiting.
FilmInCollectionResponse.title: FilmInCollectionResponse

FilmReviewResponse.description: A site's review of the film: a link, Brave's line, and Blu-ray.com's scores once read.
FilmReviewResponse.title: FilmReviewResponse

HighlightRatingResponse.description: One person's rating of a film: their highest, as "Worth a rewatch" reads it.
HighlightRatingResponse.title: HighlightRatingResponse

HighlightsResponse.description: Everything the panel shows, in one request. An empty row is left for the page to hide.
HighlightsResponse.title: HighlightsResponse

IdentificationDoubtResponse.description:
What the film page says while a doubt is open, and since Batch Y4 what either person
needs to settle it there.
IdentificationDoubtResponse.title: IdentificationDoubtResponse

IdentifyDoubtResponse.description: An identified film that may be the wrong one — Batch X9 (CT46-01, CT46-03).
IdentifyDoubtResponse.title: IdentifyDoubtResponse

IdentifyOverviewResponse.description: How many unmatched films wait, and what became of the rest.
IdentifyOverviewResponse.title: IdentifyOverviewResponse

ListingUpdateRequest.description:
Move a disc between §3.4's listing states — Batch 29, phases 4.2 and 4.4.

**One endpoint for every transition rather than a verb each.** "List for sale", "mark
sold", "mark donated" and "put it back" are the same write with a different target
state, and four endpoints would be four places to remember the audit row, the price
and the guard. Phase 4.4's acceptance turns on a transition being *recorded*, not on
which URL performed it.
ListingUpdateRequest.title: ListingUpdateRequest

ListingUrlResponse.description:
A link that opens eBay's "start your listing" form with the title filled in.

**Nothing is created by asking for this.** Phase 4.3's Option A — a Sell API draft —
does not exist as described, so the app never holds a selling credential and never
creates a live listing; the admin opens this link signed in as themselves and
publishes from eBay. `DECISIONS.md` #142.
ListingUrlResponse.title: ListingUrlResponse

LoanCreateRequest.description:
A loan names its borrower one of two ways — Batch W3 (#249).

``borrowerName`` for anyone, as before; or ``borrowerProfileId`` for one of the people
who use the app ("I'm borrowing it"), whose name the server fills in. Exactly one.
LoanCreateRequest.title: LoanCreateRequest

LocationResponse.description:
Where one of a film's live copies sits.

``label`` is composed server-side so every surface says "Front 2nd" the same way,
rather than each of the three collection views inventing its own join of the two
columns.
LocationResponse.title: LocationResponse

MaybeOwnedFilmResponse.description:
An owned film with no TMDB id yet whose title reads as this one — Batch X10.

Search's "Might be your copy of …" (T2), asked by the add form too.
MaybeOwnedFilmResponse.title: MaybeOwnedFilmResponse

MaybeOwnedResponse.description: An owned film with no TMDB id yet whose title reads the same as this result.
MaybeOwnedResponse.title: MaybeOwnedResponse

MoveCopyRequest.description: One copy is another film — Batch X9.
MoveCopyRequest.title: MoveCopyRequest

MoveCopyResponse.description: Where the copy went, and the audit row that undoes the move.
MoveCopyResponse.title: MoveCopyResponse

MovieNightSessionResponse.description:
One sitting.

`inviteToken` is returned **only to people already in the session**. It is the whole
credential for joining — the same reasoning as Batch 27's gift slug — so an endpoint
that leaked it would be an open door with extra steps.
MovieNightSessionResponse.title: MovieNightSessionResponse

NavSectionsResponse.description:
How many rows stand behind each destination that hides itself when empty.

**Counts rather than booleans**, deliberately. A boolean answers "show this?" and
nothing else; a count lets the sidebar show a number later without a second endpoint
and a second round of cache invalidation, and it makes a wrong answer legible in the
response rather than opaque.
NavSectionsResponse.title: NavSectionsResponse

NoteRequest.description: What a person types on the You page.
NoteRequest.title: NoteRequest

NotificationPreferenceResponse.description: §6.1's toggles as the settings page reads them.
NotificationPreferenceResponse.title: NotificationPreferenceResponse

NotificationPreferenceUpdateRequest.description:
A partial update — every field optional, absent means unchanged.

``quietHours`` is the exception: the two ends move together or not at all, because a
start without an end is a window that never closes. The migration's CHECK says the
same thing; this says it with a 422 instead of a 500.
NotificationPreferenceUpdateRequest.title: NotificationPreferenceUpdateRequest

NotificationResponse.description: One row of the outbox, as the notifications page shows it.
NotificationResponse.title: NotificationResponse

OnThisDayMemoryResponse.description: One of the caller's viewings on this calendar day in a prior year.
OnThisDayMemoryResponse.title: OnThisDayMemoryResponse

PendingToolCallResponse.description:
A write Claude asked for and has **not** performed.

The input is included in full because §9.4's prompt has to say what will actually
happen — "Claude wants to use a tool" is not a decision anyone can make.
PendingToolCallResponse.title: PendingToolCallResponse

PhotoResponse.description:
One photo's metadata.

**No bytes.** A gallery of five photos would otherwise be a megabyte of base64 in a
JSON list, re-fetched on every render; the browser asks for `url` instead and gets a
cacheable image with an `ETag`.
PhotoResponse.title: PhotoResponse

PriceEstimateResponse.description:
What a title is currently being *asked* for on eBay UK — Phase 4.1.

Never what it sold for. Marketplace Insights is closed to new applicants and eBay put
sold listings behind a login wall in late August 2026, so sold comps are unobtainable
(`DECISIONS.md` #16, re-confirmed by #126). `basis` carries the exact words every
surface must show.
PriceEstimateResponse.title: PriceEstimateResponse

PriceSegmentResponse.description:
One comparable group of current listings.

**`sampleSize` is not optional and never will be.** A median over three listings and a
median over sixty look identical on a card, and `DECISIONS.md` #129 is an account of a
number that looked perfectly reasonable and was 149% high. The UI is required to show
this beside the price.
PriceSegmentResponse.title: PriceSegmentResponse

PurgePreviewResponse.description: What a 90-day purge would destroy. ``dryRun`` is the default, deliberately.
PurgePreviewResponse.title: PurgePreviewResponse

PushDeviceStatusRequest.description: Batch X3: "does the server hold this browser's subscription?" — by its endpoint.
PushDeviceStatusRequest.title: PushDeviceStatusRequest

PushDeviceStatusResponse.description:
What the server holds for this browser, for the signed-in person.

``live``: it pushes here. ``refused``: the push service refused it, so the page registers
the phone again, with a fresh subscription. ``removed``: the person took it off their
list, so the page leaves it alone. ``unknown``: the server has no such device for this
person, so the page registers it.
PushDeviceStatusResponse.title: PushDeviceStatusResponse

PushSubscriptionCreateRequest.description:
Register this browser. The body is the browser's own subscription JSON, plus a label.

Taking the browser's shape verbatim rather than flattening it means the client posts
``{...subscription.toJSON(), deviceLabel}`` and nothing has to be transcribed — which
is one fewer place for ``p256dh`` to be mistyped into a subscription that encrypts to
nobody and still gets a 201 from the push service.
PushSubscriptionCreateRequest.title: PushSubscriptionCreateRequest

PushSubscriptionKeys.description: The ``keys`` object exactly as ``PushSubscription.toJSON()`` emits it.
PushSubscriptionKeys.title: PushSubscriptionKeys

PushSubscriptionResponse.description:
One registered device.

**The endpoint is not returned in full.** It is a bearer capability — anyone holding
it can push to that device — and the UI only needs enough to tell two rows apart.
PushSubscriptionResponse.title: PushSubscriptionResponse

ReminderRunResponse.description: What one reminder pass found and queued.
ReminderRunResponse.title: ReminderRunResponse

ReviewScoreResponse.description: One score under the site's own heading: "Movie", "Video 4K", "Overall".
ReviewScoreResponse.title: ReviewScoreResponse

RewatchSuggestionResponse.description: A personally highly rated film whose latest viewing is no longer recent.
RewatchSuggestionResponse.title: RewatchSuggestionResponse

RewatchedFilmResponse.description: A film watched twice or more, counted across both diaries.
RewatchedFilmResponse.title: RewatchedFilmResponse

ScrapeRunRecordResponse.description:
One recorded run — §5.5's acceptance in the numbers it is stated in.

**`attempted` already excludes `notStocked`** — `DECISIONS.md` #107: a shop that
answered honestly and has not got the film was not an attempt that failed. This
docstring used to say the denominator was "attempted minus notStocked", and the page
believed it, so a real run of 17 attempted against 23 not-stocked rendered as
"Nothing to price" over six priced discs (#125).

The denominator #112's corrected criterion compares `written` against is `attempted`
minus **`noResults`** alone: everything else in `attempted` was a pair somebody could
have priced. `failures` is the criterion's "logged with retailer + reason".
ScrapeRunRecordResponse.title: ScrapeRunRecordResponse

ScraperTestRequest.description:
§5.4's "test scraper" — run selectors against a page and show what they matched.

**This makes the server fetch a URL a person typed**, which is why `services/scraping/
fetcher.py` resolves the host and refuses anything not publicly routable. Admin-only,
but the realistic risk is a paste or a typo reaching the container's own loopback
interface, not malice.
ScraperTestRequest.title: ScraperTestRequest

ScraperTestResponse.description:
What the selectors matched, and whether it looks like a price.

``ok`` is **not** "the request succeeded" — it is "this looks like a real price for
this film". A page that fetched perfectly and yielded a plausible-looking wrong number
reports ``ok: false`` with the reason, which is the entire point of §5.4 existing
before a retailer is enabled.
ScraperTestResponse.title: ScraperTestResponse

SendRequest.description:
Batch T4, snag 11 — who to send tonight to.

Omitted, it means everyone who is not in the night yet. In a two-person app that is
"the other person", which is the one-tap case the snag asked for.
SendRequest.title: SendRequest

SessionCreateRequest.description: §8.3's "session creation with filters", in Batch 12's smart-collection shape.
SessionCreateRequest.title: SessionCreateRequest

ShopPriceResponse.description: A shop's latest price for a want (Batch X11, MK47-05).
ShopPriceResponse.title: ShopPriceResponse

SmartCollectionFilters.description:
The complete, closed vocabulary a saved collection may constrain on.

**These are exactly the query parameters ``GET /movies`` accepts**, by name and by
type, and that is the point: a saved collection is a saved filter-bar state, so
anything expressible here must mean the same thing there. ``extra="forbid"`` is what
keeps an unrecognised key from being persisted and then quietly ignored at
evaluation — a collection that silently drops half its criteria would list the wrong
films with total confidence.
SmartCollectionFilters.title: SmartCollectionFilters

SmartCollectionResultsResponse.description:
A page of films, plus the collection that produced it.

Deliberately the same ``items`` shape as ``GET /movies`` so the results page can
reuse the grid rather than growing a second card component that renders the same
film differently.
SmartCollectionResultsResponse.title: SmartCollectionResultsResponse

SpecAcceptRequest.description: One of the offered pages, or a Blu-ray.com release address Craig pasted.
SpecAcceptRequest.title: SpecAcceptRequest

SpecBackfillStartResponse.description: What pressing "Run a batch now" did. Only ``started`` searches or fetches anything.
SpecBackfillStartResponse.title: SpecBackfillStartResponse

SpecCoverageResponse.description: Where the ~1,250 Blu-ray and 4K discs stand.
SpecCoverageResponse.title: SpecCoverageResponse

SpecsFetchRequest.description: A batch of targets. **Makes live requests to Blu-ray.com.**
SpecsFetchRequest.title: SpecsFetchRequest

SpecsRunResponse.description: What a run did. **Every URL fetched is listed** — the ledger requires that.
SpecsRunResponse.title: SpecsRunResponse

SpecsStateResponse.description:
Whether the integration is running, and what it has done.

`halted` is the state #110 makes sticky: a `403`, a `429` or an objection stops
everything, and only an owner decision starts it again.
SpecsStateResponse.title: SpecsStateResponse

SpecsTargetRequest.description: One disc and the release page it is described by.
SpecsTargetRequest.title: SpecsTargetRequest

SpendPoint.description: Cumulative spend at a point in time, for §13.1's "collection value over time".
SpendPoint.title: SpendPoint

SuggestionRequest.description: Put a film forward. **Exactly one of `movieId` and `tmdbId`.**
SuggestionRequest.title: SuggestionRequest

SyncRunResponse.description:
One sync, in the shape the panel reads.

**`startedAt` is the field the UI actually needs.** The 50-entry feed cap makes the
*interval* a correctness property (`DECISIONS.md` #159), so "when did this last run"
is the question, and a sync that failed still answers it — `error` says why.
SyncRunResponse.title: SyncRunResponse

TestNotificationResponse.description:
What §6.2's test button did.

``delivered`` is the count of devices that actually took the push, so "I pressed test
and nothing happened" separates into *no devices*, *the push service refused*, and
*it was delivered and your browser did not show it* — three different problems.
TestNotificationResponse.title: TestNotificationResponse

TmdbSearchResultResponse.description: A film the add form found on TMDB but the catalogue does not have yet.
TmdbSearchResultResponse.title: TmdbSearchResultResponse

ToolCallResolveRequest.description: `confirm: false` is a real answer, not an absence of one.
ToolCallResolveRequest.title: ToolCallResolveRequest

ToolListResponse.description: §9.2's acceptance, made directly observable: ask as an admin, ask as a viewer.
ToolListResponse.title: ToolListResponse

ToolSummary.description:
One tool this person may use.

`writes` is on the wire because §9.4's prompt is the visible consequence of it, and a
UI that has to guess which tools ask for confirmation will guess wrong eventually.
ToolSummary.title: ToolSummary

TopRatedRowResponse.description: Films on the shelf rated 4½ or 5 stars, and whose ratings those are.
TopRatedRowResponse.title: TopRatedRowResponse

TrashItemResponse.description: One soft-deleted row, as §13.5's trash lists it.
TrashItemResponse.title: TrashItemResponse

TrashRowResponse.description:
One soft-deleted row, in a shape that reads the same whatever table it came from.

§13.5 lists items "per table", and four tables with four response shapes would mean
four list components. ``label`` and ``sublabel`` are composed server-side so the trash
is one list.
TrashRowResponse.title: TrashRowResponse

TrialAsking.description: The asking price from the same search, by the valuation's own rule.
TrialAsking.title: TrialAsking

TrialBids.description: The auctions in the same search.
TrialBids.title: TrialBids

TrialBlendTotal.description: Bids where a film has a bid price, asking prices otherwise.
TrialBlendTotal.title: TrialBlendTotal

TrialFilm.description: One film and format in the sample, and what its search found.
TrialFilm.title: TrialFilm

TrialResults.description: What the search returned, before any judging.
TrialResults.title: TrialResults

TrialStoredPrice.description: The film's stored value, from the last valuation run: asking prices only.
TrialStoredPrice.title: TrialStoredPrice

TrialSummary.description: The trial's answer for one format, or for all of them (``formatCode`` null).
TrialSummary.title: TrialSummary

TrialTotal.description: What the films add up to on one basis, and how many discs stand behind it.
TrialTotal.title: TrialTotal

UsageResponse.description: §9.7's counters, as the settings page and the chat header show them.
UsageResponse.title: UsageResponse

UsedValueResponse.description:
What one disc on the shelf is worth as a used copy — Batch X6 (#256).

``basis`` says how: ``used``, the median of ``sampleSize`` used listings; ``new_scaled``,
New's median of ``sampleSize`` listings times ``factor``, the used-to-New ratio measured
for the format, because used listings were too few. ``low`` and ``high`` are the range of
those listings before any factor.
UsedValueResponse.title: UsedValueResponse

UserRole.description: Craig administers, Mark views. Both can read the collection.
UserRole.title: UserRole

UsernameRequest.description:
Letterboxd's own username alphabet, mirrored from the CHECK on the column.

**A public username, never a credential** (`DECISIONS.md` #161).
UsernameRequest.title: UsernameRequest

UsualSourceResponse.description: One part of an eBay find's usual price (Batch V8): eBay's figure, or a shop's.
UsualSourceResponse.title: UsualSourceResponse

ValuableDiscResponse.description: An owned film and format at its stored value, with what the value rests on.
ValuableDiscResponse.title: ValuableDiscResponse

ValuationStartResponse.description: What pressing "Update values" did. Only ``started`` spends anything.
ValuationStartResponse.title: ValuationStartResponse

VapidKeyResponse.description:
The application server's public key, for ``pushManager.subscribe``.

Served rather than shipped as a build-time `VITE_` variable — see the note on
:class:`src.config.Settings`. ``configured`` is false when Railway has no key, which
is the state that produced the TMDB outage: a feature that is simply absent, with the
front end unable to say so.
VapidKeyResponse.title: VapidKeyResponse

VoteResponse.description:
The result of one swipe.

`match` is non-null only on the swipe that *completes* one, so the browser can show it
immediately without waiting for the event stream to come back round.
VoteResponse.title: VoteResponse

WantedCreateRequest.description:
Add a film to the wanted list — §5.1.

Either a ``movieId`` for something already catalogued, or a ``tmdbId`` for something
that is not. The second is what makes §11.2's "bulk add missing to wanted list" and
§7.2's recommendation cards work at all: **the whole point of wanting a film is that
you do not own it**, so requiring it to exist in `movies` first would exclude every
realistic case.
WantedCreateRequest.title: WantedCreateRequest

WatchHistoryStatusResponse.description: Everything the panel shows before anybody presses anything.
WatchHistoryStatusResponse.title: WatchHistoryStatusResponse

WatchedByResponse.description:
One other participant who has seen this film, and when — Batch S7.

`DECISIONS.md` #157's fourth point. **Everyone except the person asking**: "have I
seen it" is on the film's own page; what a card needs to say is whether the people you
are choosing with have.
WatchedByResponse.title: WatchedByResponse

src__schemas__movie_night__CandidateResp.description:
A film on tonight's list.

**Batch S7 made this a suggestion rather than a deal from the deck.** `movieId` is null
for a film outside the Archive — those can be suggested now, and carry their own title
and poster because there is no `movies` row to read them from.
src__schemas__movie_night__CandidateResp.title: CandidateResponse

get.description:
§13.2's feed — "last 20 events across all users".

**Two of the four sources §13.2 names do not exist yet.** Price drops are Batch 20 and
loans are Batch 15; both add their rows to this endpoint when they land. What is here
is real: watches from `watch_log`, and every admin write from `admin_actions`.

Additions come from the audit log rather than from ``collection_items``, and the
difference matters: ``added_at_utc`` is NULL on all 1,857 imported rows and
``created_at`` is the import timestamp, so ordering the feed by the item table would
put 1,857 identical "added" events at the top and bury everything else forever.

The audit log, newest first.

``movieId`` is what §3.11's condition history on the detail page uses: it resolves
to every one of that film's discs — **including soft-deleted ones**, because the
history of a disc that was thrown away is exactly the history worth keeping.

post.description:
§9.1 — ask one question. §9.7 — refuse gracefully once the cap is reached.

**The cap is checked before the call, not after.** Checking afterwards would still
have spent the money, which is the only thing the cap exists to prevent.

**A refusal is a 200, not a 429.** §9.7 asks for a "graceful limit reached message" and
the person needs to read it in the chat where they asked; an error status hands the
front end an exception to render instead of an answer. The body says `blocked` and
carries the sentence.

get.description:
§9.3's "conversation detail", plus anything still waiting to be confirmed.

The pending calls are part of the detail because a person can close the tab on a
confirmation prompt and come back — the row outlives the stream that raised it.

post.description:
§9.3's acceptance — *"user sends message, streamed response renders progressively"*.

Answers `text/event-stream`. `X-Accel-Buffering: no` is not decoration: a proxy that
buffers the body delivers the whole answer at once, which looks exactly like streaming
being broken and is invisible in every test that does not run behind that proxy.

get.description:
The caller's own usage log — what was asked of the model and what it cost.

Not the transcript: the prompts and answers are not stored here, only the accounting.
Batch 31 adds conversations, and keeping them apart is what lets this survive one
being deleted.

Can this deployment answer a question at all?

post.description:
§9.4 — confirm or cancel a pending write, then continue the turn.

**Nothing has run at this point.** The write executes here if and only if `confirm` is
true; cancelling records the refusal and tells the model the write did not happen, so
it cannot go on to report success.

get.description:
§9.2's acceptance — *"the tool list differs correctly between admin and viewer"*.

An endpoint rather than an internal detail, because that criterion is a statement about
what a given person can do and the only honest way to check it is to ask as them.
§9.7's counters for today.
The problems the last daily check found, oldest first, and whether it is running.

post.description:
A line from the person asking, for Craig's "Needs attention" (Batch X12a).

Open to both people, so it works for Craig too; the You page offers it to Mark.

delete.description: Craig has read it. The row stays in the table, cleared, as a record.

post.description:
Revoke a refresh token. Idempotent — an unknown token is not an error.

Only the opaque half is needed to find the row, and the signed half is deliberately
not verified: signing out must still revoke a token whose signature has expired.
Until 23 Sep 2026 this split at the first dot, like ``refresh``, so it never found a
row and no sign-out ever revoked anything (`DECISIONS.md` #200).

Mark the setup wizard finished.

Idempotent, and deliberately **keeps the first timestamp**: re-running the wizard
from settings later should not rewrite when this person actually got set up. Phase
2.8 asks for the flow to be skippable, and skipping to the end is still finishing —
the wizard offers nothing that has to be done, so there is no half-complete state to
represent.

Set or change the caller's own PIN. Never anybody else's.

Reachable only with a valid access token, which for a profile in the seeded
``pin_hash = NULL`` state means the first PIN is set through an admin-minted token
rather than by anyone who knows the display name.

Exchange a refresh token for a new pair, revoking the one presented.

Rotation on every use: the presented row is revoked before the replacement is
issued, so a token used twice fails the second time even within its 30-day life.

**Both halves are checked.** The opaque half finds the row; the signed half must verify
against the refresh secret and name that same row and that same person. Until 23 Sep
2026 the signed half was never read, and the opaque half was read wrongly, so no
renewal ever succeeded (`DECISIONS.md` #200, :func:`src.auth.split_refresh_token`).

Record what a barcode turned out to be — §3.4's confirmation, persisted.

**This adds no disc.** It writes the mapping so the *next* scan of the same code is
instant and certain; adding the disc is the existing `POST /collection`, which the
client calls with the confirmed film. Keeping them apart means a confirmation that is
right about the film but wrong about the shelf does not have to be undone twice.

§3.4's chain: cached mapping → the collection → eBay Browse → TMDB.

**Amazon is not the third leg, and that is a correction rather than an omission.**
`DECISIONS.md` #91 ruled it out permanently in September 2026 — it blocks automated
access and its Product Advertising API is unsuitable here. `docs/phase-batches.md`
records the substitution.

**Each leg stops the chain when it answers**, because the legs are in order of
certainty and cost. A confirmed mapping and a disc already owned are both free and
both certain; eBay costs a unit of a 5,000-a-day quota; TMDB costs a call and can only
be asked once something has produced a title.

**An empty result is an answer.** §3.4's second half is *"unknown UPCs prompt manual
search"*, so nothing matching returns 200 with no candidates — never a 404, which the
client would have to special-case into the same screen anyway.

get.description:
Every live box set with its completion status — §11.4's acceptance criterion.

Unpaginated on purpose. The whole point of the grid is that it shows *all* of them
with status, and the ceiling is the number of physical boxes on the shelves — a
couple of dozen, against 1,857 discs. A page control here would hide sets behind a
"next" button for no benefit.

post.description: Create a box set, optionally with its discs — §11.3's acceptance in one call.

delete.description:
Soft-delete the grouping. The discs are untouched.

Soft because the row groups real objects and the realistic mistake is deleting the
wrong set. Nothing surfaces these in the trash yet — §13.5's Trash is Batch 15, and
widening ``TRASH_TABLES`` is that batch's job.

get.description: Serve one private photo hero to a signed-in person only.
Upcoming releases, soonest first — §6.5's `/calendar`.

The unauthenticated iCal feed — §7.4.

``request`` is unused by the body and required by slowapi's decorator, which reads the
client address off it.

**A wrong token and a revoked token get the same 404**, with the same body. A 401, or a
different message for "this used to work", would confirm to someone guessing that a
token had once existed — and there is no user to tell apart from an attacker here,
because the whole point is that nobody signs in.

post.description:
§7.3's ingestion, on demand — the same refresh a stale read starts, now.

Admin-only: it spends a shared TMDB budget and writes a table both people read. Since
Batch T5 the calendar also refreshes itself when read and more than a day old, so this
is the "now, please" button rather than the only way it ever updates.

get.description:
§7.4's monthly view, bucketed by day server-side.

Grouping here rather than in the browser keeps the grid a rendering problem, and makes
an empty month an explicit empty map rather than something the client infers.

post.description:
Issue this person's feed URL — §7.4's "subscribe button with copy-link".

**Calling this again rotates the link**, revoking the previous one. That is the whole
recovery story for a URL pasted somewhere it should not have been, and the response
says so, so nobody is left believing two links work.

Add one disc, refusing an unconfirmed duplicate with 409.

The 409 carries the existing copies, so a client that skipped
``/collection/duplicate-check`` still gets everything §3.5's prompt needs and the
confirmation cannot be bypassed by not asking.

get.description:
The warning §3.1 wants *before* saving.

A read, so the add form can ask as soon as a film is chosen rather than discovering
the clash by being rejected. ``POST /collection`` enforces the same rule
independently — this endpoint is the courtesy, not the guard. The one exception is
``maybeOwned``: an unidentified film that may be this one is a question for the person,
so only this check asks it.

The vocabulary the filter bar offers, counted from the data.

Serving it rather than hard-coding it is what keeps the shelf picker honest: it can
never offer "Front 7th" because no such shelf exists, and it cannot miss a shelf
that a newly added disc has just created. Genres and formats stay static in the web
app because those are closed vocabularies; where 1,857 discs actually live is not.

post.description:
Move many discs in one request — Batch Y2 (`DECISIONS.md` #265).

Either person, as editing is since #264. **Partial success:** each disc is checked on
its own against the version it was picked at (#42), so one changed on the other phone
is reported ``stale`` and left alone while the rest move. Every place is resolved
before anything is written, so an unknown section refuses the whole request rather
than half of it. One ``update`` audit row per disc that moved, with the same diff an
edit writes, so each film's history shows the move.

get.description:
§13.1's dashboard, in one request.

One request rather than six, because six would make the page's load time the slowest
of six round trips and the charts appear one at a time.
Every owned physical disc at its stored price, and how many have one.
The latest bid trial and its report, finished or not; null before the first.

post.description: Start a bid trial within today's share, after the response. It saves no prices.

Start pricing the films that are due, within today's share, after the response.

The run is claimed before the response, so the answer is definite: ``started`` means a
run exists and is this one. Anything else starts nothing and spends nothing.
Craig starts the first live pass; subsequent passes run in the existing eBay job.

delete.description:
Soft-delete one disc — §3.2's "move to trash".

Either person may delete (#264); only the admin may list the Trash or restore from it,
so a disc Mark removes by mistake is Craig's to bring back.

Sets ``deleted_at`` directly rather than issuing a ``DELETE``. The
``collection_items_soft_delete`` trigger would turn a ``DELETE`` into this same
update, but going through the trigger would leave the session holding an object it
believes is gone, and the row it must be refreshed from is the one being returned.

Returns the item rather than 204 so the client can show what it just removed and
offer an undo without a second round trip.

put.description:
Replace the editable fields of one disc, logging the diff.

Either person may edit, which is also how a disc moves shelf (`DECISIONS.md` #264,
superseding #37): Mark adds discs since #155, and a disc he could add but not correct
was the gap. The audit row names whoever acted.

Also §3.11's "mark as damaged" quick action: the client already holds the whole
copy, so setting one field and re-submitting is the same request. A second endpoint
for it would be a second place for the condition timestamp to be forgotten.

post.description:
The edition the spec job inferred is this copy's — Batch X9 (CT46-05).

Either person, as an edit is (#264). The page stops saying "probably", and the audit row
says who looked at the box.

put.description:
Move a disc between §3.4's listing states — phases 4.2 and 4.4.

**Sold is not deleted, and that distinction is the batch.** §4.4 asks that marking
sold *"removes from active views, remains in audit/trash"*, and the obvious reading —
soft-delete it, so the existing trash machinery hides it — is wrong for one reason
that only shows up in ninety days: §6.30 **auto-purges the trash after 90 days**
(`services/trash.py`). A sold disc routed through `deleted_at` would be permanently
destroyed a quarter later, taking the record of what it fetched with it.

So the row stays, undeleted, and ``owned_copy()`` is what removes it from the active
views — see that predicate for the nineteen places the word "owned" was previously
spelled out. "Remains in audit" is this function's audit row; "remains in trash" is
unchanged, because a sold disc can still be deleted and restored like any other.

**`listed_for_sale` stays visible.** A disc that is advertised is still a disc on the
shelf until somebody buys it; hiding it at the moment of listing would make listing
indistinguishable from losing.

get.description: §3.10's gallery, as metadata. The bytes come from `/photos/{id}`.

post.description:
Upload one photo. Resized before it is stored — see `services/photos.py`.

**Read with a ceiling, not with `await file.read()`.** An unbounded read pulls whatever
was sent into memory before anything has had a chance to refuse it, which is a
denial-of-service in one line.

get.description:
§5.10's filters: genre, discount %, retailer, format.

**Dismissed deals are excluded and there is no way to ask for them.** §5.10's
acceptance is *"dismissed items don't reappear"*, and an `includeDismissed` flag
would be a way for them to. Putting one back is
`POST /deals/{id}/dismiss {"dismissed": false}` — an act, not a view.

Genre is filtered in Python rather than in SQL. `movies.genres` is a JSONB array of
objects, and the containment query that would do this in Postgres needs a GIN index
this table has no other use for — against a feed capped at 200 rows, the join is
already the expensive part.
How many live deals there are, for the nav badge.

post.description:
§5.9's run. **Dry by default, because this hits real shops.**

The same default `POST /scrapers/run` carries, for the same reason: a live run against
somebody else's website is something a person should have to ask for twice.

The response carries the criterion's own three numbers — rows written, retailers that
produced any, and how many were skipped as already owned — so the acceptance can be
read off it rather than inferred.

§5.10's one-tap dismiss — and its undo.

**A soft state, not a delete.** Tonight's scrape will re-find the same deal on the
same URL, so "doesn't reappear" has to be something the row remembers; a deleted row
would simply be re-created. `deals_runner._upsert` preserves this column for exactly
that reason.

get.description:
§7.2's "new releases feed filtered by collected genres".

Every result says *which* of the collection's genres put it there. A suggestion that
cannot explain itself is indistinguishable from a random one.

Answer eBay's validation challenge.

eBay sends this GET immediately when the endpoint is saved, and again periodically to
confirm the endpoint is still alive.

post.description:
Acknowledge a deletion notification.

**Deliberately a no-op.** The app stores no eBay user identifier anywhere — Batch 28's
``price_checks`` rows hold a listing's price, title and URL, none of which is keyed to
an eBay account — so there is nothing to erase when one closes. Acknowledging is still
mandatory: an endpoint that stops answering is an endpoint eBay reports as down.

**Still true since T8b** (`DECISIONS.md` #245). "Connect eBay" keeps each person's two
tokens, sealed, and no eBay identity: the account's name is read live and never stored,
so a notification names nothing this app could look up. A closed account's tokens stop
working, and the app deletes them the moment eBay refuses one.

**The body is not read and the signature is not verified, because nothing acts on
either.** eBay signs these with a key retrievable from its Notification API, and if
this handler is ever given real work to do, verifying that signature is the first thing
to add — an unauthenticated POST that deleted rows would be a hole. Today it deletes
nothing, so there is no privilege for a forged notification to exercise.
Finish a sign-in this person started, with the code eBay sent them back with.
Begin connecting: a one-time state, and eBay's consent address to go to.

get.description: This person's listings for sale and their last 60 days of sales, read from eBay now.
This person's watch list and saved searches, read from eBay now.

post.description:
Phase 4.3 — the pre-filled listing link, and what to ask for the disc.

**Option B promoted to primary.** Option A, a Sell API draft listing, describes
something eBay does not do: an Inventory API offer is invisible until published, at
which point it is a live listing with a buyer on the other end. `DECISIONS.md` #142.

**No eBay call is made unless a price is wanted.** The URL is built locally; the
suggested price needs a search, so this asks for one only when a format is given —
which is the case where the number means something.

Phase 4.1 — a median per segment, with the sample size and the rejections.

**A POST rather than a GET, and not for tidiness.** A film title in a query string ends
up in access logs and proxy caches; more practically, this spends a unit of a 5,000-a-day
production quota, and a GET invites a browser, a prefetcher or a retry to spend it again.

**Sandbox cannot prove this endpoint** — its GB catalogue is empty — so Phase 4.1's
acceptance, *"querying 'Blade Runner 2049 Blu-ray' returns a reasonable UK median
price"*, is a live production call and therefore the owner's, per
`docs/agent-commands/group-start.md`. What ships here is the whole path plus its tests
against two captured 200-listing payloads.

A price alert on any UK Buy It Now listing of a film on a format. No eBay call.

``download=true`` sends it as a file; the default renders it in the tab, which is

A film card for something the collection does not hold — Batch T2.

One TMDB call: details, credits and watch providers arrive together through

``merge``; undone from the recent list, which opens the doubt again.

Every set with its owned/missing counts — §11.2's acceptance criterion.

Ordered by how close each set is to complete, so the page opens on the ones worth
finishing rather than on an alphabet.

post.description:
Rebuild the sets from TMDB — §11.1's refresh, on demand.

**"Weekly" is not implemented here and deliberately so.** Scheduling belongs to the
platform, and adding a Railway cron is a hosting change this project keeps explicit.
This endpoint and `src/scripts/refresh_completion_sets.py` are what a schedule would
call; wiring the schedule is an owner action.

get.description: One set's films, owned first — §11.2's "missing films list with posters".

§12.5's loans page — "active and past loans", per §6.5.

Open loans first, soonest due first. Readable by both people: knowing where a disc
went is not an admin question, even though lending one is.

post.description:
§12.5's acceptance: "Lending a disc shows it in Loans".

**Either person lends or borrows** since Batch W3 (`DECISIONS.md` #249): Mark lends the
discs as much as Craig does, and Craig borrows them. A borrower who is one of the two is
named by ``borrowerProfileId`` and their name is filled in from it; anyone else is a
name. The audit row records who made the loan either way.

**No push is sent from here, and that is deliberate.** §12.5's second clause is
"overdue triggers a push" — a statement about a *due date passing*, not about a disc
being lent, so it belongs to the scheduled pass rather than to this handler.
`notify_overdue_loans` in `services/reminders.py` owns it as of Batch 11, and writes
the `loans.reminder_sent` column this table has carried unused since Batch 15.

post.description: §8.3 — start a movie night. The creator is its first participant.

§8.3's acceptance — *"second user joins via URL"*.

**Authenticated, unlike Batch 17's feed and Batch 27's gift page.** Those are read-only
surfaces for people with no account; this one votes, and a vote has to belong to
somebody. The token says *which session*, not *who*.

get.description:
Tonight's list — **Batch S7 rebuilt this from a deck into a shortlist.**

Batch 35 dealt each person a random hand of films from the collection and hid what
they had swiped. `DECISIONS.md` #157 replaced the input side: anyone suggests, everyone
sees the same list, and a film outside the Archive can be on it.

**The card answers "what is this and have they seen it"** before a swipe — cast,
runtime, genres, where it streams if nobody owns it, and which of the *other*
participants have watched it and when.

post.description:
Batch T4, snag 11 — one tap sends tonight to the other person.

It puts them in the night, so it is already in their list before they open anything,
and it pushes a notification that opens this night rather than the app's front page.
One push per person per night: sending twice does not buzz a phone twice. Their
notification settings and quiet hours apply, as to every other push.

Put a film forward — `DECISIONS.md` #157's first and second points.

**Anyone in the session, and any film.** Not admin-gated and not restricted to the
Archive: a movie night where one person may not name a film is not one, and the point
of allowing films nobody owns is that "shall we rent something" is a real answer.

§8.4 — one swipe, and the match if it completed one.

**Cast on a suggestion since Batch S7**, not on a film: that is what lets everyone vote
on anyone's suggestion and what lets a film with no `movies` row be voted on at all.

get.description:
The discs owned for this film — and, on request, the ones that have gone.

**`includeSold` exists so §4.4's "removes from active views" does not mean
"unreachable".** A sold disc keeps its row (`collection.update_listing_status`
explains why it is not soft-deleted), and this is the one surface that can show it:
everywhere else, "owned" is what the word means. Default false, so every existing
caller keeps the active view it already had.

get.description:
§7.2 — TMDB's recommendations, flagged against what is on the shelf.

§7.2's acceptance asks for "10+ recommendations with correct ownership flags". TMDB
returns 20 per page for a well-known film and can return **none** for an obscure one;
the endpoint reports what there is rather than padding, because a padded list would
make the flag meaningless.

§7.1 — where this film can be streamed, in the caller's region.

The region comes from the profile and can be overridden per request, which is what
makes "is this on Netflix at my sister's in Ireland?" answerable without changing a
setting.

Row counts for the destinations that hide themselves when empty.

Each count matches what its page would actually list, which is the property that
matters: a menu item that appears and then leads to an empty page is the bug this
endpoint exists to prevent, and it would be a subtle one — the item would be *right*
about the table and *wrong* about the page.

The caller's outbox, newest first.

This is the page that answers "why did I not get that": a suppressed row names the
category that was off, and a queued one shows the morning it is waiting for.

post.description: Push everything queued and due, without running the reminder senders.

get.description: §6.1's toggles, created with everything on if this is the first read.

put.description: Change some of §6.1's toggles. Absent fields are left alone.

post.description:
Run every reminder sender, then deliver whatever is due.

``asOf`` is what makes §5.11's acceptance testable — *"test date set 2 weeks before a
seeded event triggers a reminder"* — and it is also how a missed day is caught up.
It cannot be pushed into the future beyond today, because reminding somebody about a
sale that has not been announced is not a feature.

**This endpoint is the whole scheduler.** There is no in-process timer: `DECISIONS.md`
#60 already settled that an in-process scheduler is worse than nothing here, because
a second container silently doubles every reminder. A Railway cron calling this is the
hosting step Batch 20 stops for.
§5.11's seeded data, for one year. Idempotent — re-running adds nothing.

get.description: This person's registered devices — §6.2's per-device records.

post.description:
Register this browser, or refresh the registration it already has.

**Upsert on the endpoint, not insert.** A push service hands back the same endpoint
when a browser re-subscribes, so a plain insert would give one device two rows and
every future push two copies. The conflict target is the unique index migration 020
creates for exactly this.

An endpoint that moves between people — the same browser, a different login — is
reassigned rather than refused: the device is whoever is signed into it now.

Batch X3 (DS44-02): what the server holds for this browser's subscription.

The page asks on every open and when the worker reports a subscription change, and
registers the phone again when the answer is ``unknown`` or ``refused``. Before X3 the
page read only the browser's own subscription, so Settings said "Notifications are on
for this device" above "No devices are registered yet", and nothing ever re-registered.
A device of another person's reads ``unknown``: registering reassigns it, as it always has.

delete.description:
Unregister one device — §6.2's "removing one doesn't silence the other".

Scoped to the caller, so one person cannot unsubscribe the other's phone. Revoked
rather than deleted, so the row can still explain a push that stopped arriving.

post.description:
§6.2's test-notification button, aimed at **one** device.

Aiming it at one device rather than all of them is what makes the criterion testable:
"both receive pushes" and "removing one doesn't silence the other" are questions about
individual devices, and a button that sprays every device cannot answer either.

The test bypasses quiet hours and digest mode deliberately — pressing a button and
being told the push will arrive at nine tomorrow is not a test of anything — but it
does **not** bypass the category toggles, because there is no category to switch off.

get.description:
The public key a browser needs to subscribe.

**Derived from the private key rather than read from its own variable.** Two variables
can disagree; a derived one cannot. If Railway holds only the private half, this still
answers correctly — and if it holds neither, ``configured: false`` lets the UI say
"push is not set up on the server" instead of failing at ``subscribe()`` with a
``DOMException`` nobody can act on.

delete.description:
§3.10's "deletion works".

**A hard delete, unlike most of this app.** §13.5's Trash exists for things somebody
might want back, and it restores *rows*; a soft-deleted photo would keep its bytes in
the database for ever, which is the one cost this whole batch is arranged to avoid.

get.description:
The bytes, cacheable.

A strong `ETag` and a conditional `304` mean a gallery re-render costs nothing, and
Batch 8's service worker can store the response. `private` because a photo of somebody's
shelves is not for a shared cache to hold.

post.description: §5.2's acceptance: "Admin adds a new retailer; it's saved and enabled".

§5.2's "seeded default retailers", as an action rather than a migration.

**Not seeded by migration `016`,** deliberately: a migration that inserts rows makes
`downgrade` ambiguous (does it delete rows an admin has since edited?) and CI's
migration job cannot prove either direction. As an idempotent endpoint it can be run,
re-run and inspected.

**Every seeded retailer has an empty `scraper_config`.** The CSS a real page needs is
Batch 19's work, and inventing selectors here would be worse than none: the ledger's
own risk note for Batch 19 says a wrong selector *"does not error — it selects the
wrong node and persists a plausible wrong number"*. An empty config is visibly
unconfigured.

§5.8's roll-up on its own, without a scrape.

`olderThanDays` is what makes the acceptance — *"after backdating test data, rows > 90
days are aggregated and raw rows removed"* — checkable without waiting a quarter or
trusting a fixture's idea of what four months ago was.

Copy the built-in selectors onto the matching seeded retailers.

Separate from Batch 18's seeding on purpose. A seeded retailer is a name and a URL — a
fact. Selectors are a **guess** until someone runs them, so putting them on requires a
deliberate second action, and the response still reports every one as unverified.

get.description:
Every built-in configuration, and which of them anybody has actually run.

``unverified`` is the four sources that cannot be scraped from here — HMV and CEX
disallow the search routes, Amazon blocks automated access, Blu-ray.com lists
third-party prices — reported so the settings page says so rather than implying they
work. The ledger's risk note for this batch is that a wrong selector does not error,
it persists a plausible wrong number.

post.description:
§5.5's nightly pass — **the endpoint a Railway cron calls.**

*Since #119 the cron runs `src.scripts.daily_scrape` instead, so this is "Run now" on
/retailers, and it does not wait for a shop that asks (Batch 20b, second half).*

Scrape, alert on anything that has just fallen to or below its `max_price`, deliver
what is queued, then roll up whatever is now older than `retentionDays`.

**`dryRun` defaults to `false` here, unlike `/scrapers/run`.** That endpoint is a tool
a person points at live shops and its safe default is to write nothing; this one is a
scheduled job whose entire purpose is to write, and a cron that quietly did nothing
every night would be the worst possible failure — indistinguishable from working.

There is no in-process schedule behind it (`DECISIONS.md` #60): one container's timer
becomes two runs the moment the service scales, against real shops.

Every enabled retailer × every active wanted item. **Makes live requests.**

``dryRun`` defaults to **true**: this endpoint hits real shops, and the version that
writes should be the one you ask for rather than the one you get by forgetting a
parameter. Running it for real is §5.3's acceptance and therefore an owner action.

get.description:
Recent runs, newest first — how §5.5 is checked the morning after.

Readable rather than merely logged, because on 2026-09-09 a scraper "test" displayed
results while saving nothing and there was no way to tell afterwards.

post.description:
§5.4 — run selectors against a page and show what they matched.

**`ok` means "this looks like a price for this film", not "the request worked".** A
page that fetched perfectly and yielded a plausible wrong number reports `ok: false`
with the reason, which is the whole reason §5.4 exists before a retailer is enabled.

This is the one endpoint in the app that fetches a URL a person typed. See
`services/scraping/fetcher.py` for why that is checked per redirect hop.

get.description:
Films that match a search and are **not** on the shelf — Batch T2, snag 14.

``GET /search`` answers "do we own it, and where is it?". This answers the rest: what
else goes by that name, where it streams, and whether it might be one of ours that
nothing has identified yet. A film with a live disc never appears here; it is
``/search``'s, and showing it twice would be the duplicate the criterion forbids.

The caller's own collections, in sidebar order.

``pinned=true`` is what the dashboard asks for — §6.31's "can be pinned to the home
dashboard" — rather than the dashboard fetching everything and filtering in the
browser, which would ship the whole sidebar to render three tiles.

Evaluate the saved filters now — §11.5's "lists correct films and updates live".

Nothing is cached and nothing is stored. The page is produced by
:func:`src.routers.movies.movie_page`, the same function behind ``GET /movies``, so
"Unwatched 4Ks from the 2010s" saved here and typed into the filter bar are the same
query by construction rather than by agreement.

delete.description:
Remove every field derived from Blu-ray.com.

**This is the endpoint that makes #110's acceptance reversible.** The owner accepted the
risk partly on the basis that *"deletion remains an explicit owner action"* and that
every derived row records its source — this is the action, and `specs_source_url` is what
makes it possible to find them.

Only rows that actually came from there are touched: a spec typed in by hand has no
source URL and is left alone. **An edition goes only when it is the one the page names**
(Batch U2): one typed or corrected by hand stays.

get.description: How far the backfill has got across the ~1,250 Blu-ray and 4K discs, and its spend.

post.description:
One batch now, rather than tonight: the same budgets, rules and halt as the job.

Claimed before the response, so ``started`` means this batch exists. It then searches
and fetches after the response, which can take a quarter of an hour.

§3.7 — fetch specs for a list of discs. **Makes live requests to Blu-ray.com.**

Each `sourceUrl` was already checked against #110's bounds by the request model, so a
search URL or another host is a 422 before anything leaves the building. Requests are
sequential and spaced; a `403` or `429` halts the whole integration and abandons the
rest of the batch.

Stop it, now.

Here because #110 names *"an explicit objection"* as a halt condition alongside the HTTP
ones, and an objection arrives in an email rather than a status code. One button.

**There is deliberately no endpoint that un-halts.** #110: *"resuming after any of those
requires a new owner decision."* A decision is a `DECISIONS.md` entry and a deliberate
database change, not a button somebody can press twice by accident.

get.description: Discs waiting for Craig to pick a page, paste one, or skip.

post.description: Craig's choice of page for one disc. Nothing is fetched now: the next batch does it.
No specs for this disc.

get.description: Is the integration running, what has it fetched, and how much data is derived?

Find a film that is not in the catalogue yet.

``GET /search`` answers "do we already own this?"; this answers "what is this disc I
am holding?". Each result says whether the catalogue already has that TMDB id, so
the add form can attach to the existing film rather than creating a second row for it.

Soft-deleted discs, newest first.

§13.5 widens this to every soft-deleting table; this batch serves the one it
deletes from, and rejects the others rather than answering "nothing here" for a
table it has not implemented.

§13.5's "list soft-deleted items per table", with every table's count for the tabs.

A separate path from Batch 7's `/trash`, which serves only `collection_items` and is
what the existing trash page and the offline queue already call. Replacing that
endpoint's shape would have broken both for a rename.

post.description:
§6.30's 90-day purge, **on demand and dry by default**.

"Auto-purged" would be a cron, which is a hosting change this project keeps explicit
(`DECISIONS.md` #60) — and a timer that permanently destroys rows is the last thing to
add without a person deciding to. ``dryRun`` defaults to **true** so the destructive
call is the one you have to ask for, not the one you get by forgetting a parameter.

Put a soft-deleted disc back, with everything it had.

§13.5's acceptance is *"restoring brings it back with full state"* — which holds
here because a soft delete never cleared anything. Clearing ``deleted_at`` fires the
derived-field trigger's UPDATE branch, so the film's ``best_format_owned`` comes
back with it.

delete.description:
**Irreversible.** §13.5's permanent delete, and the first one in this app.

Only a row already in the trash can be destroyed. That makes it a deliberate two
steps — delete, then destroy — rather than one mis-tap away from losing a disc's
history for good.

The audit row is written **before** the delete and in the same transaction, because
afterwards there is nothing left to describe. `admin_actions.target_id` is TEXT with
no foreign key so the entry outlives its subject (`DECISIONS.md` #5).

post.description:
§13.5's acceptance: "restoring brings it back with full state".

Only ``deleted_at`` is cleared. Every other column is exactly as it was, because a
soft delete never removed them — a restore is not a re-create, and treating it as one
is how a restored row comes back subtly different from the one that was deleted.

get.description: §5.1's list. Readable by both people.

post.description:
§5.1's acceptance: "adding to wanted list from detail page ... works".

Batch V9: once the response has gone, Brave is searched for the film's reviews on
Blu-ray.com and AVForums, so the links are there when the list is next opened.

delete.description:
Soft-delete, so §13.5's Trash can restore it — the tab Batch 15 built and could not
fill.

get.description:
What the panel shows before anybody presses anything.

**The last run is the point.** The feed carries 50 entries and no more, and Mark
cycles his in about eight weeks, so a sync that silently stopped running would lose
history without ever failing (`DECISIONS.md` #159).

post.description:
Fetch this person's diary feed and write whatever is new.

**Reuses S8's matcher and writer whole** — the feed reader's only job is to produce the
same `DiaryEntry` the file import produces, so a viewing present in both sources
becomes exactly one row (`DECISIONS.md` #176).

**Does not identify films**, even though every feed entry carries a TMDB id. That
rewrites `movies` rows, which is the operation S8 put in the owner's hands; doing it
from a button on a schedule would make it happen quietly and repeatedly instead.

put.description:
Set or clear **your own** Letterboxd username.

Caller-scoped with no admin override: there is no reason for one person to set the
other's, and every reason not to have the endpoint that would allow it.

get.description:
The caller's own history, newest first, optionally for one film.

``movieId`` is what the detail page uses to show "you watched this on …" without a
second endpoint that would answer the same question in a second shape.

delete.description:
Soft-delete one of the caller's own entries.

Soft, because §13.5 sends deleted watch logs to Trash — and because the realistic
failure here is a mis-tap on a phone, which should not permanently lose the record
that someone watched something.

A 404 rather than a 403 for another user's entry: whether a given id exists in
someone else's history is not something this response should confirm.
